funnel.name: common gates
funnel.text: Common hard filters of every mission: elevation_m >= 1.0 (Earth only); mask_fraction >= 0.3 (both bodies). Failing one eliminates the cell for the mission.

funnel.name: required variables
funnel.text: Every variable in the mission's require_present list must have a value; a missing one eliminates the cell with the reason '<variable> no data'.

funnel.name: mission hard filters
funnel.text: The mission's own gates (missions[].gates, with their limits); failing one eliminates the cell for that mission (no score, no rank), with the exact reason, e.g. '<variable> outside [<min>, <max>]'. An eliminated cell may still pass another mission.

funnel.name: suitability
funnel.text: Survivors only: suitability = 100 * sum(w * u) / sum(w over weighted variables with a value); utility u runs linearly from 0 at 'bad' to 1 at 'good', clipped (tables for classes); contribution = w * u; a missing weighted variable is ignored and the remaining weights renormalised; coverage = weight with a value / total weight.

funnel.name: similarity
funnel.text: rover, solar: similarity on real values (similarity.json real_value): per variable s = exp(-0.5 * (|earth - moon| / tolerance)^2) (Rover: s = 1 within the measurement uncertainty sigma of the elevation models, else exp(-0.5 * max(0, |d| / sigma - 1)^2); similarity.json real_value score_by_mission), similarity = 100 * weighted mean of s; the twin is the lunar zone cell with every key variable within 1 x its tolerance and every secondary within 2 x its tolerance that has the highest similarity; a point with no such cell has no twin, no similarity and no final (it keeps its suitability). lunar_base: similarity on thermal position and real terrain (missions.json similarity, rule percentile_and_real_tolerance): the variables with scale 'percentile_within_population' are compared as their percentile within their own population (Earth: the points passing the mission's funnel; Moon: the cells of the zone), the others in real values; per variable s = exp(-0.5 * (difference / tolerance)^2), similarity = 100 * weighted mean of s; the twin is the zone cell with every key variable within 1 x its tolerance and every secondary within 2 x its tolerance that has the highest similarity; a point with no such cell has no twin, no similarity and no final (it keeps its suitability). A likeness of position, not of equal values: the real values are shown with every pair.

funnel.name: final
funnel.text: final = alpha * similarity + (1 - alpha) * suitability (alpha in missions.json 'alpha'); survivors with a similarity are ranked by the published final, ties by Earth cell id; survivors without a twin (real-value missions) follow, by published suitability, ties by Earth cell id.

elimination_line_rule: the cell's reason codes (fail_bits) in bit order, their 'text' joined with '; '

known_limitations: The rover thresholds (slope 0.5-15 deg, roughness 5-650 m) were written for a 300 m baseline and are applied unchanged to km-baseline values (slope over about 3.7-3.8 km, roughness at a lag of about 1.9 km). km-baseline slopes are much gentler than rover-scale slopes and km-lag roughness is larger than 300 m roughness, so passing these gates says nothing about rover-scale hazards. Nothing was adjusted (known limitation, pending Robotics 1).

Similarity is computed on real values within stated tolerances, on slope and roughness only, 50 % each (decision of 2026-11-15 11:23 CET): the twin is the cell of the lunar south-polar zone (75-90 S) whose slope is within 2 deg and roughness within 30 m of the Earth cell (illustrative values of the team's rover file for a 5 km baseline), with the highest similarity. Relative elevation is no longer compared (it has no physical sense for a rover); it is shown per pair as a difference. A point with no such cell keeps its suitability but has no twin, no similarity and no final score.

Relative elevation, temperature, diurnal amplitude and irradiance are not part of the rover similarity: their values on both sides and the difference are shown for information (the lunar south-polar twins are colder than their Earth points by a median of about 150 K).

The list is ordered by the final score: 50 % similarity to the lunar twin and 50 % suitability for the mission. These are five of the 254 sites tied at the top of our model, chosen to be spread across the world, not a proven best.

How stable these five are: under the documented uncertainty of the input data (200 simulations), number 1 is among the five shown in 52.5 % of the simulations and stays in the group tied at the top in 72.5 %; number 2 is among the five shown in 43.0 % of the simulations and stays in the group tied at the top in 43.0 %; number 3 is among the five shown in 65.0 % of the simulations and stays in the group tied at the top in 88.5 %; number 4 is among the five shown in 87.5 % of the simulations and stays in the group tied at the top in 100.0 %; number 5 is among the five shown in 67.0 % of the simulations and stays in the group tied at the top in 74.0 %. The exact same five come back in 10.5 % of the simulations (60 different fives in all). Under a change of plus or minus 10 % in any one weight, each of the five stays among the five shown in 10 of the 10 weight changes. The five are a sample of close candidates, not a fixed answer. The lunar twin of each of the five is kept in 17.5 to 38 % of the simulations, and the group tied at the top keeps about 89 % of its members (median). In plain words: which five are shown is not stable, because many sites are tied at the top and any of them could be shown; which sites belong to the tied group mostly is.

Ice sheets are not excluded: the funnel has no surface-type gate and the soft criteria have no surface-type term. 1,506 of the 10,337 ranked points are ice-sheet or snow-and-ice cells (snow and ice cover at least half of the cell, or the thermal class is ice); the best of them is number 1,089, 0 are in the top 50 and 0 among the five shown. Water is not excluded either: 1,145 ranked points are cells whose single commonest land-cover class is water in the ESA CCI land-cover map (sea along a coast, or lakes); the best is number 1, 12 are in the top 50 and 0 among the five shown (none).

Rover compares slope and roughness only. No further terrain variable is measured on both bodies, defined alike, meaningful for mobility and independent of these two: Diviner rock abundance, the obvious candidate, has a value in 0 of the 5,400 cells of the Rover lunar zone, and nothing equivalent exists for Earth.

With slope and roughness alone, many sites differ from their lunar twin by less than the measurement error of the elevation models (ETOPO 2022 and LOLA), and such differences are scored as equal, so 254 of the 10,337 paired sites share the top final score of 100.00. These are five of the 254 sites tied at the top of our model, chosen to be spread across the world. The tie is within the measurement uncertainty of the elevation models (slope 0.27 degrees, roughness 17.4 m): the data cannot tell these sites apart. How the five are chosen among them: a cell half or more snow and ice is left out, and so is a cell less than half land (241 tied sites remain); the first is the remaining tied site with the highest similarity, then each next one is the tied site farthest from those already chosen, so the five are at least 2 degrees apart (the closest two are 60.0 degrees apart). The full ranking itself is unchanged.

In the Rover suitability, slope (45 %) and roughness (30 %) are nearly one criterion: over the 10,337 passing points their utilities have a Spearman correlation of 0.97. The team's weights are kept unchanged.

The Rover suitability is saturated too. 250 of the 254 sites tied at the top score the maximum on every one of the team's Rover criteria (slope (degrees) 45 %, full marks at 1 or less; roughness (m) 30 %, full marks at 30 or less; bare-ground share 25 %, full marks at 0.7 or more), so the team's criteria do not tell them apart either (253 of the 10,337 ranked points show a suitability of 100.00). Points that reach the maximum of each criterion, among the 10,337 ranked: slope (degrees) 3,291; roughness (m) 2,144; bare-ground share 930; all three: 250. Among the 254 tied sites: slope 0.500 to 0.961 degrees, roughness 14.61 to 30.19 m, bare-ground share 0.707 to 1.000. Worked example: Bardenas Reales (number 7,046, similarity 100.00, suitability 70.43): slope (degrees) 1.91, utility 0.93, 2.9 points lost; roughness (m) 77, utility 0.92, 2.3 points lost; bare-ground share 0.0176, utility 0.03, 24.4 points lost; Tabernas Desert (number 7,390, similarity 100.00, suitability 69.36): slope (degrees) 3.17, utility 0.85, 7.0 points lost; roughness (m) 111, utility 0.87, 3.9 points lost; bare-ground share 0.146, utility 0.21, 19.8 points lost; against the first analog shown (number 3, similarity 100.00, suitability 100.00): slope (degrees) 0.77, utility 1.00, 0.0 points lost; roughness (m) 29.3, utility 1.00, 0.0 points lost; bare-ground share 0.868, utility 1.00, 0.0 points lost. The criteria as the team wrote them reward the gentlest, barest ground and say nothing else about mobility (a recognised badlands analog with some vegetation cover loses about a quarter of its score on the bare-ground share alone); this is a weakness of the suitability criteria, left as written and to be examined by the re-audit.

The Rover minimum slope of 0.5 degrees is a criterion of the team with no official source. It is kept because of its measured effect: without it 7,847 more points pass (2,862 of them ice or snow cells), 26 of the top 50 would be added points, all of them flats with a slope below 0.5 degrees (water-dominated cells in the top 50 go from 12 to 25), one lunar twin takes 16.4 % of the pairs instead of 2.6 %, and the known mobility analogs rank worse (Qaidam from the top 4.0 % to 8.3 %, Haughton 4.2 % to 8.4 %, Ramon 3.6 % to 8.0 %, Yungay 8.1 % to 11.6 %).

known_limitations: The Solar panels similarity is saturated. Sunlight above the atmosphere depends on latitude only, so almost every Earth point finds many cells of the equatorial maria that match it almost exactly: its twin is the best of a median of about 1,840 candidate cells that pass the tolerances, 78 % of the 6,360 pairs score 99 or more and 514 show 100.00. Here a high similarity says that the pair is within the tolerances, not that it is closer than another pair: read the real differences shown beside it (sunlight above the atmosphere, slope and roughness). Among the 100 best-ranked points the similarity only goes from 99.00 to 100.00, so their order follows suitability.

The solar twin is matched on sunlight above the atmosphere (team decision of 2026-11-15, morning): Earth's annual-mean sunlight at the top of the atmosphere (DERIVED from latitude) against the lunar surface irradiance of the equatorial maria (|lat| <= 30 deg, elevation <= -1,200 m), within 0.6 kWh/m2/day, with slope and roughness as secondary criteria. Only part of that sunlight reaches the ground on Earth (shown per pair); on the Moon all of it does, in a lunar day of 29.5 Earth days. The maria receive the sunlight of Earth's tropics, so only points within about 33.5 deg of the equator find a twin; the others keep their suitability with no twin.

Earth irradiance at the ground and sun geometry no longer weigh in the suitability: the ground irradiance only filters (a cell needs 2.5 kWh per square metre a day or more) and so do the sun-geometry gates. The suitability criteria are clear-sky fraction (0.35), slope (0.15), daily temperature swing (0.1) and roughness (0.1). Earth irradiance at the ground is surface solar energy under the atmosphere and clouds (WorldClim) and lunar irradiance is airless geometry; the solar gates on irradiance, maximum sun elevation and low-sun fraction would remove the lunar cells nearer the poles (shown only when a lunar cell is inspected: lunar cells are not filtered for the similarity).

Temperature and diurnal amplitude are not part of the solar similarity: their values on both sides and the difference are shown for information. 6,060 passing solar cells (all in Antarctica) have no land surface temperature: the amplitude weight drops out of their suitability with the remaining weights renormalised. None of them has a lunar twin (they lie at 64.5 S or further south, far from the latitudes whose sunlight matches the maria), so they have no similarity, no final score and no confidence.

The list is ordered by the final score: 50 % similarity to the lunar twin and 50 % suitability for the mission. These are five of the highest-scoring analogs in our model, not a proven best: the five best final scores once a cell half or more snow and ice, a cell less than half land and a point within 2 degrees of one already chosen are skipped (numbers 1, 2, 5, 7 and 9 of the full ranking).

How stable these five are: under the documented uncertainty of the input data (200 simulations), number 1 stays in the top 5 in 9.5 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 40.0 %; number 2 stays in the top 5 in 7.0 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 37.5 %; number 3 stays in the top 5 in 13.0 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 31.5 %; number 4 stays in the top 5 in 1.5 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 14.5 %; number 5 stays in the top 5 in 0.5 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 12.5 %. The same five come back together in 0 of the 200 simulations. Under a change of plus or minus 10 % in any one weight, each of the five stays among the five shown, with the same twin, in 14 of the 14 weight changes. The five are a sample of close candidates, not a fixed answer.

The Solar panels suitability no longer uses criteria driven by latitude. The maximum sun elevation and the share of time with a low sun (pure geometry of latitude) and the modelled ground irradiance (WorldClim, which repeats what the similarity already compares) carry no weight now; their gates still apply, and the ground irradiance, the sunlight above the atmosphere and the share lost stay in every pair's sentence. In their place, the clear-sky fraction measured by satellite makes up half of the suitability (50 %: its weight 0.35 out of the 0.70 that the four weights add up to; the suitability is divided by that sum): 1 minus the mean ISCCP-H cloud amount (NOAA NCEI, monthly means 2012 to 2016), scored from 0 at 0.308 to 1 at 0.671, the 10th and 90th percentiles over the 18,777 points that pass the funnel. 3 of those points have no cloud value and that weight is shared among the other criteria. One of them, the cell at 4.5 S 122.5 E (in Sulawesi, Indonesia, number 16 in the full ranking, suitability 96.23), ranks that high only because its clear-sky weight is shared among the other criteria; it is not among the five shown.

known_limitations: The Lunar base criteria are an exact copy of the team's thermal block (team design values, no external source). The ice block is shown per Earth cell as information only (passes or not, its suitability) and never changes this ranking; no lunar cell passes ice because the lunar permafrost class is the MODELLED label 'none', which the ice gate excludes.

Similarity is a likeness of thermal POSITION and real terrain, not of temperature (team decision of 2026-11-15 08:55 CET): the coldest temperature and the daily temperature swing are compared as percentiles within each population (Earth: the points passing this mission's funnel; Moon: the cells of NASA's nine candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole), each within 10 percentile points, and slope and roughness in real values (within 4 deg and 60 m). Equal positions do not mean equal temperatures: on every pair the twin is far colder and swings far more than the Earth point, and the real values and differences are shown with every pair. A point with no such cell keeps its suitability but has no twin, no similarity and no final score.

The coldest temperature is a MODELLED air temperature on Earth (WorldClim, coldest month, interpolated) and a MEASURED surface temperature on the Moon (Diviner night minimum); the Earth diurnal amplitude is a difference between two satellite overpasses and understates the daily range. Both are suitability criteria on Earth, and in the similarity only their position within each population is compared, never their values.
Antarctica has no land surface temperature product here, so its cells fail for lack of a daily temperature swing value ('no data').

The list is ordered by the final score: 50 % similarity to the lunar twin and 50 % suitability for the mission. These are five of the highest-scoring analogs in our model, not a proven best: the five best final scores once a cell half or more snow and ice, a cell less than half land and a point within 2 degrees of one already chosen are skipped (numbers 1, 3, 5, 6 and 7 of the full ranking).

How stable these five are: under the documented uncertainty of the input data (200 simulations), number 1 stays in the top 5 in 18.0 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 51.5 %; number 2 stays in the top 5 in 23.0 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 52.5 %; number 3 stays in the top 5 in 19.0 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 43.5 %; number 4 stays in the top 5 in 18.0 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 38.0 %; number 5 stays in the top 5 in 22.5 % of the simulations and in the top 20 in 59.0 %. The same five come back together in 0 of the 200 simulations. Under a change of plus or minus 10 % in any one weight, number 1 stays in the top 5 in 16 of the 16 weight changes, number 2 in 16, number 3 in 15, number 4 in 15 and number 5 in 10. The five are a sample of close candidates, not a fixed answer.

The Lunar base keeps the team's gate 'daily thermal swing at least 15 K'. Without it, Earth cells with a swing of about 1 K (for example on Ellesmere Island) would match the Moon's coldest temperature at a similarity of about 99, and the key variable, the thermal swing, would carry no weight in practice. The recognised polar stations therefore do not pass: daily land-surface swing Haughton crater (Devon Island) 2.5 K; Svalbard, Bockfjorden 1.2 K; Kangerlussuaq, ice-sheet margin 6.6 K; McMurdo and Concordia have no land-surface temperature in the table. They are analogs of cold and isolation, not of thermal cycling.

The Lunar base suitability uses one criterion for the ground instead of two: the bare-or-sparse fraction (from ESA CCI land cover, continuous, without the urban class) weighs 25 %; the thermal-inertia class (built from the same land-cover classes) and the permafrost class (modelled, missing on 607 of 2,419 passing points, with no sourced link to a base) carry no weight. The thermal-inertia class is still required and still excludes water. The four weights left (daily temperature swing 35 %, coldest temperature 25 %, bare-or-sparse fraction 25 %, ground sunlight 10 %) sum to 95 %, and the suitability is divided by that sum, so in effect they weigh 36.8 %, 26.3 %, 26.3 % and 10.5 %.

top5.rule: The five shown are chosen down the full ranking by final score: a point whose cell is half or more snow and ice, or less than half land, is skipped, and so is a point within 2 degrees of arc (about 222.4 km) of one already kept. The full ranking itself is unchanged.
